title: Gene Expression and Regulation
tagline: Every cell in your body carries the same genome, yet a neuron is not a liver cell. This course is about the dials that make the difference.
overview: This course follows information from DNA to protein and asks, at every step, who decides how much. We start with the logic of regulation in bacteria (RNA polymerase, sigma factors, operons, attenuation and the lambda switch), then move to the far richer machinery of eukaryotes: RNA polymerase II, enhancers and transcription factors, chromatin and epigenetic marks, RNA processing and splicing, microRNAs and RNA decay, translational control and regulated protein degradation. The final unit connects the machinery to hormones, development and disease. The units follow the standard content of a BSc Honours gene-expression course.
whyItMatters: Almost every question in modern biology and medicine, from how a stem cell becomes a neuron to why a tumour grows, is at heart a question about which genes are on, how strongly and for how long. Drugs, diagnostics, RNA vaccines and gene therapies are all built on this knowledge.
studyTips: Draw each regulatory system as a wiring diagram (input, sensor, switch, output) before memorising names; most exam questions are really 'what happens if this wire is cut'.
For every factor you meet, ask three things: what does it bind, what does it recruit, and what does that change (transcription, splicing, stability, translation)?
Learn the classic experiments as logic puzzles: mutant phenotype in, inference about mechanism out. The lac operon mutants are the best practice you will ever get.
Keep a one-page comparison table of bacteria versus eukaryotes for each stage (promoter, polymerase, processing, coupling of transcription and translation).

units.title: From gene to function: the levels of control
units.hook: Your liver cell and your neuron share one genome, one set of instructions, and yet they could hardly look or behave more differently. The secret is not which genes you own but which ones you read, and every step between DNA and a working protein is a place where the reading can be turned up, down or off.
learningObjectives: Describe the flow of genetic information and name the checkpoints at which expression can be regulated
Distinguish constitutive (housekeeping) from regulated genes and give an example of each
Explain why transcription initiation is the most common point of control
Compare the organisation of gene expression in bacteria and eukaryotes
Describe the main experimental readouts of expression (RNA-seq, qPCR, reporter assays, western blots)

keyConcepts.definition: The principle that sequence information flows from DNA to RNA to protein; later additions such as reverse transcription do not overturn it, they add routes.
A gene needed in essentially all cells (for example those for ribosomal proteins or glycolytic enzymes) that is expressed at a fairly steady level.
A gene whose product level changes with cell type, developmental stage or environmental signal.
A DNA sequence on the same molecule as the gene it controls (promoter, operator, enhancer) where regulatory proteins bind.
A diffusible molecule, usually a protein or RNA, encoded elsewhere that acts on cis elements; mutations in the two classes behave differently in genetic tests.
In bacteria ribosomes start translating an mRNA while it is still being made; in eukaryotes the nuclear envelope separates the two processes and adds processing and export steps.
The amount of an mRNA or protein is the balance between its synthesis rate and its degradation rate, so changing either one changes the level.

deeper.beginner: Think of the genome as a huge cookbook that every cell owns a copy of. A cell never cooks every recipe at once; it picks the ones it needs, in the amount it needs. Gene regulation is the system of bookmarks, sticky notes and kitchen timers that decides which recipes get cooked. Control is possible at many stages: whether a gene is copied into RNA, how that RNA is trimmed and edited, how long it survives, how often it is read by ribosomes and how long the finished protein lasts. The analogy breaks down because a cookbook is passive, whereas the 'sticky notes' here are themselves made from genes and so regulate each other.
deeper.intermediate: Because transcription is the first and most economical step, many genes are controlled mainly there: making an RNA that is then thrown away costs less if it is never made. Even so, mRNA level alone does not predict protein level well, since translation rate and protein half-life differ greatly between genes. Bacteria rely on short-lived mRNAs and compact operons for fast responses, whereas eukaryotes add chromatin, enhancers, splicing and nuclear export, giving more layers and more combinatorial possibilities. Experimentally, expression is measured at the RNA level by qPCR and RNA-seq, at the transcription level by reporter genes such as luciferase or GFP fused to a promoter, and at the protein level by western blots or mass spectrometry.
deeper.advanced: Expression is a kinetic system. If mRNA is made at rate k_s and degraded with first-order constant k_d, the steady-state level is k_s/k_d and the time to reach a new steady state after a change depends on k_d alone, which is why fast-responding genes (immediate early genes, stress genes) typically have unstable mRNAs. Transcription in single cells occurs in stochastic bursts, so a population mean hides cell-to-cell noise that regulatory circuits can either suppress (negative autoregulation) or exploit (bistable switches). Genome-wide studies show that mRNA abundance explains only part of the variance in protein abundance, implicating translational efficiency and protein turnover as independent controls; any claim about regulation therefore needs measurements at the level you are claiming.

commonMistakes: Assuming that a higher mRNA level always means more protein; translation and degradation can decouple them.
Treating regulation as only 'on/off'; most genes are tuned over a continuous range.
Confusing cis and trans: a mutation in a promoter is cis to its own gene only, whereas a mutation in a repressor protein affects every copy of its targets.

selfCheck.question: A bacterial gene is transcribed at twice the normal rate but its protein level rises only slightly. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: The protein is rapidly degraded or poorly translated
The gene has a new promoter
selfCheck.explanation: Protein level depends on translation efficiency and protein half-life as well as on transcript level, so a faster transcription rate need not raise the protein proportionally.

selfCheck.question: A mutation in a promoter that stops transcription of one allele but not the other allele in the same cell is acting:
selfCheck.explanation: A cis-acting element only affects the DNA molecule it sits on; a defect in a diffusible factor would affect both alleles.

selfCheck.question: At steady state, the mRNA level of a gene is set by:
options: Synthesis rate divided by degradation rate constant
Only the strength of the promoter
The length of the poly(A) tail alone
selfCheck.explanation: Steady-state level equals the production rate divided by the first-order decay constant, so both transcription and mRNA stability contribute.

units.title: Bacterial transcription: RNA polymerase, sigma factors and termination
units.hook: A single bacterial RNA polymerase must find the right few hundred base pairs among millions, start at exactly the correct nucleotide, and stop where it should. It does this with a little help from a replaceable subunit, the sigma factor, which works like a changeable key that decides which doors the enzyme can open.
learningObjectives: Describe the subunit composition of bacterial RNA polymerase core and holoenzyme
Explain how sigma factor recognises the -10 and -35 promoter elements
Outline initiation, open complex formation, abortive initiation, promoter escape and elongation
Compare intrinsic (hairpin) and Rho-dependent termination
Explain how alternative sigma factors reprogram transcription during stress

keyConcepts.definition: RNA polymerase with subunits alpha (two copies), beta, beta-prime and omega; it can synthesise RNA but cannot recognise promoters accurately.
Core enzyme plus a sigma factor; the sigma subunit confers promoter specificity.
Sequences upstream of the start site; in E. coli the consensus hexamers are about TTGACA at -35 and TATAAT at -10, and spacing and closeness to consensus set promoter strength.
The state in which about a turn of DNA around the start site has been melted so the template strand can enter the active site.
Repeated synthesis and release of short RNAs of a few nucleotides before the polymerase escapes the promoter.
A GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of uridines in the RNA; the hairpin and weak rU-dA pairing destabilise the elongation complex.
A hexameric RNA helicase/translocase that binds C-rich rut sites on nascent RNA and chases the polymerase to dislodge it.
A sigma subunit that directs core enzyme to a different promoter class, for example sigma-32 for heat shock genes and sigma-S for stationary phase.

deeper.beginner: RNA polymerase is the machine that copies a gene into RNA. On its own it slides along DNA without knowing where genes start. Binding of a sigma factor turns it into a promoter-seeking version: sigma recognises two short landmarks upstream of a gene, the polymerase unwinds a small bubble of DNA and begins to build RNA. Once it has made a short stretch, sigma usually lets go and the enzyme moves on. At the end of a gene, either the RNA folds into a hairpin that shakes the polymerase off or a protein called Rho catches up and pulls it off. The 'changeable key' picture is useful but imperfect, since sigma is not only a key; it also helps open the DNA.
deeper.intermediate: Promoter recognition proceeds from a closed complex (DNA still double-stranded) through isomerisation to an open complex; the rate-limiting steps differ between promoters and are what regulators exploit. During initial transcription the polymerase stays anchored at the promoter and scrunches DNA, which builds up the energy needed to break contacts and escape; failures give abortive products. Sigma-70 family members share conserved regions that contact the -10 and -35 elements, and the extended -10 and UP elements (bound by the alpha C-terminal domains) tune strength. Sigma-54 is exceptional: its holoenzyme forms a stable closed complex and needs an ATP-driven activator bound at an enhancer-like site. In termination, intrinsic terminators need no protein, whereas Rho depends on a C-rich, unstructured rut site and on a stretch of untranslated RNA, which is why in bacteria it often acts when translation has stopped early.
deeper.advanced: Single-molecule and cryo-EM work show that open-complex formation involves large conformational changes, including closing of the polymerase clamp around the downstream DNA, and that pausing during elongation (for example at consensus pause sites, with hairpin-stabilised or backtracked states) is an important regulatory node: backtracked complexes are rescued by GreA/GreB cleaving the RNA 3' end. Pausing is also coupled to translation, since a trailing ribosome can push the polymerase forward, and NusA, NusG and Rho together coordinate speed and termination. Antitermination proteins such as phage lambda N and Q modify the elongation complex so that it reads through terminators, showing that termination, like initiation, is a regulated step. Be careful with numbers: elongation rates depend on temperature and sequence, and are typically quoted as tens of nucleotides per second in E. coli.

commonMistakes: Saying that sigma factor stays bound throughout transcription; it is usually released during or soon after promoter escape, although its release is not absolute.
Mixing up the positions: -35 is further upstream than -10, and both are upstream of the +1 start.
Describing Rho-dependent and intrinsic termination as requiring the same signals; only the latter needs the hairpin and U-run.

selfCheck.question: Which subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase confers promoter specificity?
selfCheck.explanation: Core enzyme is catalytically active but non-specific; sigma binds the -10 and -35 elements and positions the holoenzyme at the promoter.

selfCheck.question: An intrinsic bacterial terminator typically consists of:
options: A GC-rich RNA hairpin followed by a run of U residues
A TATA box followed by a poly(A) signal
An AU-rich element in the 3' UTR
selfCheck.explanation: The hairpin disrupts the elongation complex while the weak rU-dA base pairs of the following U run let the transcript dissociate.

selfCheck.question: Why do heat shock genes remain transcribed when bacteria are heated?
options: Sigma-32 directs polymerase to their promoters
selfCheck.explanation: Heat raises the level and activity of the alternative sigma-32, which recognises heat shock promoters that sigma-70 does not.

units.title: Operons and bacterial regulatory circuits
units.hook: In 1961 two French scientists worked out how a bacterium decides to digest milk sugar, using nothing more than clever mutants and logic, and in doing so described the first gene regulatory circuit. The lac operon is still the best way to learn how to think about genes as switches.
learningObjectives: Explain the structure and negative and positive control of the lac operon
Predict the phenotype of lacI, lacO, lacZ and CAP mutants and merodiploids
Explain catabolite repression and diauxic growth
Describe how the trp operon uses a repressor and attenuation together
Describe the lambda lysis-lysogeny decision as a genetic switch
Name regulatory mechanisms that act at the RNA level in bacteria, such as riboswitches

keyConcepts.definition: A cluster of genes transcribed together from one promoter as a polycistronic mRNA and controlled as a unit.
A repressor protein binds an operator DNA sequence and blocks transcription; in lac the repressor is LacI and the main operator overlaps the promoter.
A small molecule that inactivates a repressor; allolactose is the natural lac inducer and IPTG is a non-metabolisable laboratory mimic.
A cAMP-binding activator that helps polymerase at the lac promoter, so that full expression needs both lactose present and glucose low.
A mutant that expresses the operon regardless of inducer, for example lacI loss-of-function or lacOc operator mutations.
A small molecule that activates a repressor; in the trp operon tryptophan binds TrpR and strengthens its operator binding.
Regulation by premature termination in a leader region, governed by whether a ribosome translating a short leader peptide stalls at tryptophan codons.
A bistable circuit in which CI repressor maintains lysogeny and Cro promotes the lytic cycle, with each one repressing the other.
A structured segment of mRNA that binds a metabolite directly and changes fold to switch transcription or translation.

deeper.beginner: Bacteria group genes that serve one purpose into a single unit called an operon, so they can all be switched on together. In the lac operon, the genes for digesting lactose are normally blocked by a repressor protein sitting on the DNA. When lactose (strictly, a derivative called allolactose) is around, it grabs the repressor and pulls it off, and the genes are read. But the cell also checks for glucose, a better food, and if glucose is present it keeps the operon quiet anyway. So the cell only makes lactose-digesting enzymes when lactose is there and glucose is not. The 'light switch' picture works for the repressor, but the CAP part is more like a dimmer that makes the lights brighter.
deeper.intermediate: Classic genetics decoded the circuit. lacI- mutants are constitutive and recessive in a merodiploid because the wild-type repressor from the other copy acts in trans; lacOc mutants are constitutive but cis-dominant because they only affect the operator on their own DNA molecule; lacIs (super-repressor) mutants cannot bind inducer and are dominant because they bind operators on both copies. Positive control adds a second layer: when glucose is low, cAMP rises, binds CAP and the CAP-cAMP complex recruits polymerase, which is why a lacI- strain still shows only low expression in glucose. In the trp operon, repression alone gives about a 70-fold range, and attenuation adds further tuning because the leader region can fold into an antiterminator (2-3) or a terminator (3-4) hairpin depending on where the ribosome is stalled. The lambda switch shows cooperative binding of CI dimers to adjacent operators and a decision triggered by DNA damage via RecA-stimulated CI cleavage.
deeper.advanced: The lac circuit also illustrates positive feedback: lactose uptake via the LacY permease is itself induced, which produces all-or-none induction in individual cells at intermediate IPTG concentrations (bistability), as shown in single-cell studies. Quantitative models treat repressor binding as a thermodynamic problem in which DNA looping between O1 and the auxiliary operators O2 or O3 strengthens repression, a fact that explains the multiple operators found in the native system. Attenuation depends on tight coupling of transcription and translation, which only exists in bacteria, so it has no eukaryotic equivalent although functionally similar logic appears in riboswitches that bind ligands cotranscriptionally and set a kinetic competition between folding and polymerase elongation. For lambda, the stability of lysogeny (flipping spontaneously only about once in many generations) arises from cooperativity and autoregulation of CI at PRM, and it shows how a genetic circuit stores a heritable cellular state without any change in DNA sequence.

commonMistakes: Saying that lactose binds the repressor; the actual inducer is allolactose, made from lactose by beta-galactosidase (IPTG is a laboratory gratuitous inducer).
Forgetting that glucose repression acts through low cAMP and CAP, not through the repressor.
Predicting lacOc as recessive; it is constitutive only for genes on the same DNA molecule (cis-dominant).
Applying attenuation to eukaryotes; it needs transcription and translation to be physically coupled.

selfCheck.question: A lacI- strain is grown with no lactose. What do you expect?
options: CAP is inactive so nothing happens
selfCheck.explanation: Without functional repressor the operator is never blocked, so the operon is transcribed regardless of inducer (subject to modulation by CAP-cAMP).

selfCheck.question: A partial diploid carries lacOc lacZ+ on one DNA molecule and lacO+ lacZ- on the other, with no inducer. Which statement is correct?
options: Both copies of lacZ are transcribed
selfCheck.explanation: lacOc is cis-dominant: it allows constitutive transcription of the lacZ+ gene on the same molecule, so active enzyme is produced even without inducer.

selfCheck.question: In the trp operon, attenuation allows transcription to continue when:
options: Tryptophan is scarce so the ribosome stalls at the leader Trp codons
selfCheck.explanation: A stalled ribosome lets the 2-3 antiterminator hairpin form instead of the 3-4 terminator, so polymerase reads through into the structural genes.

selfCheck.question: Which condition gives maximal lac operon expression?
selfCheck.explanation: The repressor is inactivated by allolactose and, with glucose low, cAMP-CAP activates the promoter.

units.title: Eukaryotic transcription: RNA polymerase II, promoters and enhancers
units.hook: A human gene may be controlled from a switch sitting tens of thousands of base pairs away, with the DNA looping so the two touch. Eukaryotic cells replace the simple on/off logic of bacteria with committees of proteins that vote on every gene.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the roles of RNA polymerases I, II and III
Describe the core promoter elements and the order of assembly of the pre-initiation complex
Explain the role of the CTD of RNA polymerase II and its phosphorylation cycle
Describe the structure of common DNA-binding domains and activation domains
Explain how enhancers, Mediator and co-activators communicate with promoters
Explain combinatorial control and give an experimental method to study it

keyConcepts.term: RNA polymerases I, II and III
keyConcepts.definition: Three nuclear polymerases: Pol I makes most rRNA, Pol II makes mRNA and many non-coding RNAs, Pol III makes tRNAs, 5S rRNA and other small RNAs.
The minimal DNA region (about -40 to +40) where the pre-initiation complex assembles; it may contain a TATA box, initiator (Inr) and downstream elements, although many promoters lack a TATA box.
TFIID (with TBP), TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIF, TFIIE and TFIIH, which together with Pol II form the pre-initiation complex at all Pol II promoters.
The C-terminal repeat domain of the largest subunit, with heptad repeats that are phosphorylated in a pattern that recruits different processing factors through the transcription cycle.
A regulatory DNA element that can act at a distance and in either orientation, binding multiple transcription factors and increasing transcription of target genes.
A large multi-subunit coactivator complex that bridges gene-specific transcription factors and Pol II.
The part of a transcription factor that reads DNA sequence, for example zinc finger, helix-turn-helix, homeodomain, bZIP or bHLH.
A separable region that recruits coactivators or chromatin-modifying enzymes rather than binding DNA.
The principle that gene expression patterns come from the particular set of transcription factors bound, so a few factors can specify many patterns.

deeper.beginner: In eukaryotes the machinery that copies a gene into mRNA is built on the spot at each gene, rather than being pre-assembled. A set of helper proteins called general transcription factors finds the start of the gene and settles the polymerase on it. On top of this basic machinery sit regulatory proteins that bind specific DNA sequences, sometimes far away, called enhancers. These proteins act like voters: some encourage the polymerase to start, others discourage it, and the gene's activity reflects the combined decision. Think of the enhancer as a remote control. The analogy breaks because the 'remote' physically touches the gene by looping the DNA.
deeper.intermediate: Assembly of the pre-initiation complex typically starts when TFIID, via TBP, recognises the promoter, followed by TFIIA and TFIIB, then Pol II with TFIIF, and finally TFIIE and TFIIH. TFIIH uses its helicase activity to open the promoter and its kinase activity (CDK7) to phosphorylate serine 5 of the CTD, which is associated with promoter-proximal pausing and capping; later, P-TEFb (CDK9) phosphorylates serine 2 to release pausing and support elongation and processing. Specific transcription factors rarely contact Pol II directly; they recruit coactivators such as histone acetyltransferases (p300/CBP), chromatin remodellers and Mediator. Enhancers work because DNA can loop, a process supported by cohesin and CTCF within topologically associating domains, and one enhancer can regulate more than one gene.
deeper.advanced: Mapping of regulatory regions with ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq has shown that most human enhancers are cell-type specific, are marked by H3K4me1 and H3K27ac, and often produce short unstable enhancer RNAs. A model of transcription in condensate-like clusters of Mediator and factors with intrinsically disordered activation domains has been proposed, though the physical details are debated. The relationship between pausing and activation matters: in metazoans a large fraction of genes show Pol II paused 30-60 bp downstream of the start site, and release rather than recruitment is then the rate-limiting step. Experiments that test regulatory function (reporter assays, CRISPR interference or deletion of an enhancer, MPRAs) are needed because binding or histone marks alone do not prove that an element regulates a gene.

commonMistakes: Believing all Pol II promoters have a TATA box; in mammals only a minority do.
Treating an enhancer as always adjacent to the gene it regulates; many act over large distances and skip the nearest gene.
Confusing DNA-binding domains with activation domains; they are separable and can be swapped between proteins in domain-swap experiments.
Saying Pol II needs all general factors to remain bound throughout elongation; several are released after initiation.

selfCheck.question: Which complex recognises the TATA box and nucleates assembly of the Pol II pre-initiation complex?
selfCheck.explanation: TBP, a subunit of TFIID, binds the TATA box and bends the DNA, creating a platform for the other general factors.

selfCheck.question: Which property distinguishes an enhancer from a promoter?
options: It can act at a distance and in either orientation
It always contains a TATA box
It is transcribed by Pol III
It must lie immediately upstream of the start site
selfCheck.explanation: Enhancers are position- and orientation-independent elements that act through DNA looping and recruitment of coactivators.

selfCheck.question: Phosphorylation of serine 2 of the Pol II CTD by P-TEFb is mainly associated with:
options: Release from pausing and productive elongation
selfCheck.explanation: Ser2 phosphorylation is a mark of elongating polymerase and helps recruit factors for elongation and RNA processing.

units.title: Chromatin and epigenetic regulation
units.hook: If you stretched the DNA from a single human cell into a line it would be about two metres long, yet it fits inside a nucleus a few micrometres wide. Packaging is not just storage: how the DNA is wrapped decides which genes can be read at all.
learningObjectives: Describe the nucleosome and the hierarchy of chromatin compaction
Explain how histone modifications are written, read and erased
Contrast euchromatin and heterochromatin and their typical histone marks
Describe the main families of ATP-dependent chromatin remodellers
Explain DNA methylation, genomic imprinting and X-chromosome inactivation
Describe methods used to map chromatin state (ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, bisulfite sequencing)

keyConcepts.definition: About 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped roughly 1.7 turns around an octamer of two each of histones H2A, H2B, H3 and H4.
A covalent mark on histone tails (acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination) that alters chromatin or creates binding sites for reader proteins.
Enzymes that add marks (for example HATs and methyltransferases), proteins that recognise them (bromodomains, chromodomains) and enzymes that remove them (HDACs, demethylases).
Compact, transcriptionally repressed chromatin typically marked by H3K9 methylation and bound by HP1; euchromatin is more open and gene-rich.
An ATP-driven complex (SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, INO80 families) that slides, evicts or exchanges nucleosomes.
Addition of a methyl group to cytosine, mostly at CpG dinucleotides in vertebrates, by DNMTs; promoter methylation is generally associated with silencing.
Parent-of-origin-specific expression of a subset of genes, maintained by differential DNA methylation.
Silencing of one X chromosome in female mammalian cells, initiated by the long non-coding RNA Xist coating the chromosome.
Transmission of gene expression states through cell division without change in DNA sequence, for example by maintenance DNA methylation.

deeper.beginner: DNA is wound around small protein spools called histones, and the whole bundle is called chromatin. Where the DNA is tightly wound the genes are hard to reach and stay silent; where it is loose, the transcription machinery can get in. Cells place chemical tags on the histones and on the DNA itself to mark which regions should be open or closed. Because some of these tags are copied when a cell divides, a liver cell's daughter cells remain liver cells. The 'spool' picture is a good start, but the spools are not static: they are constantly slid and rearranged by molecular machines.
deeper.intermediate: Different marks have characteristic meanings: H3K4me3 at active promoters, H3K27ac at active enhancers and promoters, H3K36me3 along transcribed gene bodies, H3K9me3 in constitutive heterochromatin and H3K27me3 (placed by PRC2 through EZH2) at Polycomb-repressed developmental genes. Acetylation neutralises lysine charge and recruits bromodomain proteins, so HATs generally promote and HDACs generally oppose transcription. Remodellers use ATP to reposition nucleosomes, exposing or hiding binding sites. DNMT3A and DNMT3B establish methylation patterns de novo, while DNMT1 copies them onto the new strand after replication because it prefers hemimethylated CpGs; TET enzymes oxidise 5-methylcytosine as a step in demethylation. At imprinted loci and on the inactive X, these systems combine into stable silencing.
deeper.advanced: The 'histone code' idea (combinations of marks read by dedicated modules) is a useful framework, but evidence that single marks are always causal is mixed; many marks follow rather than lead transcription, and bivalent domains (H3K4me3 with H3K27me3) in embryonic stem cells illustrate poised states that can resolve either way. Inheritance of histone marks through DNA replication is less well established than for DNA methylation: parental histones are partitioned to the daughter strands, and read-write feedback loops (for example PRC2 binding its own H3K27me3 product) can restore marks. Methods matter for interpretation: ChIP-seq depends on antibody specificity and gives population averages, ATAC-seq reports accessibility not function, and bisulfite sequencing cannot distinguish 5mC from 5hmC without additional chemistry. Be cautious when sources claim transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in mammals; evidence is limited and context-specific.

commonMistakes: Equating all histone methylation with repression; H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 are marks of active transcription.
Describing epigenetic marks as permanent; they are dynamic and reversible and can be altered by development, environment and drugs.
Saying that DNA methylation changes the DNA sequence; it adds a chemical group to the base but leaves the sequence intact (though methylated cytosine is a mutation hotspot).
Assuming chromatin accessibility alone shows a gene is active.

units.title: RNA processing: capping, splicing and polyadenylation
units.hook: The first RNA copy of a human gene is mostly editorial rubbish: long stretches of introns are cut out and the remaining exons are stitched together, often in more than one way. A single gene can therefore make several different proteins, depending on which pieces the editors keep.
learningObjectives: Describe 5' capping and 3' cleavage and polyadenylation and their functions
Outline the chemistry and spliceosome assembly steps of pre-mRNA splicing
Identify the consensus splice-site signals and the branch point
Explain how alternative splicing is regulated and how it expands the proteome
Explain RNA editing and give examples of splicing-related disease
Explain why processing is coupled to transcription by the Pol II CTD

keyConcepts.definition: A 7-methylguanosine linked to the first nucleotide by a 5'-5' triphosphate bridge; it protects the mRNA and helps in export and translation initiation.
Endonucleolytic cleavage downstream of an AAUAAA signal followed by addition of about 200 adenosines by poly(A) polymerase, with factors CPSF and CstF.
Introns are removed from the primary transcript and exons are joined to make the mature mRNA.
Introns begin with GU at the 5' splice site and end with AG at the 3' splice site, with an internal branch point adenosine and a polypyrimidine tract.
A large complex of five snRNPs (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) and many proteins that catalyses two transesterification reactions to remove an intron as a lariat.
Use of different combinations of exons from one gene, for example exon skipping, alternative 5' or 3' sites or intron retention.
Families of RNA-binding proteins that bind exonic or intronic enhancers and silencers to promote or inhibit use of a splice site.
Post-transcriptional change of the RNA sequence, such as A-to-I deamination by ADAR enzymes or C-to-U in apoB mRNA by APOBEC1.
An RNA with catalytic activity; group I and II self-splicing introns showed that RNA can catalyse reactions.

deeper.beginner: Newly made RNA in a human cell has to be edited before it can be used. A protective cap is added to the front end and a long tail of A letters to the back end. The big job is splicing: the gene is broken into pieces called exons separated by non-coding stretches called introns, and the introns have to be cut out precisely so the exons join without a single letter out of place. Choosing which exons to join is also a form of regulation, allowing one gene to produce several different protein versions. Imagine editing a film: the same raw footage can be cut into different versions. The analogy fails in that the cuts are made by the same cell machinery during transcription, not afterwards.
deeper.intermediate: The cap is added to the nascent transcript soon after initiation, and the CTD phosphorylation pattern recruits capping enzymes, then splicing factors and, near the end, cleavage and polyadenylation factors. Splicing proceeds through two transesterification reactions: the 2'-OH of the branch adenosine attacks the 5' splice site to release the exon and form a lariat, then the free 5' exon attacks the 3' splice site, joining the exons and releasing the lariat intron. U1 snRNA base-pairs with the 5' splice site, U2 binds the branch point, and the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP completes the assembly; extensive RNA-RNA rearrangements place U2 and U6 snRNAs in the catalytic core, which is thought to be ribozyme-like. Alternative splicing allows isoforms with different domains, localisation or stability, and it is controlled by SR proteins and hnRNPs together with the strength of splice sites; most human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing. Defective splicing underlies diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy (SMN2 exon 7 skipping) and some forms of beta-thalassaemia.
deeper.advanced: Exon definition, in which splicing machinery assembles across exons rather than introns, explains how short exons are recognised within very long human introns, and it makes splice-site choice sensitive to the local RNA structure and to transcription elongation rate (kinetic coupling). Many alternative events are tissue-specific and regulated by factors such as neuronal PTBP and NOVA proteins, so isoform switches contribute to differentiation. Nonsense-mediated decay couples alternative splicing to expression level when a spliced isoform introduces a premature stop codon, which means that 'unproductive splicing' is itself a regulatory mechanism. Therapeutically, antisense oligonucleotides that block splicing silencers (nusinersen for SMA) show that splice choice can be modified pharmacologically. When interpreting RNA-seq, note that detecting a splice variant does not show it is translated or functional.

commonMistakes: Saying that introns are removed from DNA; the gene still contains introns, and they are removed from the RNA.
Forgetting that the lariat has a 2'-5' linkage at the branch point.
Assuming that all exons are always included; alternative splicing means inclusion varies between tissues or conditions.
Treating poly(A) tail addition as templated by DNA; the A residues are added by polymerase without a template.

units.title: Post-transcriptional control: mRNA decay, microRNAs and non-coding RNAs
units.hook: In 1998 a pair of scientists injected double-stranded RNA into worms and found that it silenced a matching gene far more strongly than anyone expected. That accident revealed an entire layer of regulation in which small RNAs police the messages of the cell.
learningObjectives: Describe the main pathways of mRNA decay and their regulation
Explain the roles of AU-rich elements and RNA-binding proteins in controlling mRNA stability
Outline microRNA biogenesis and how miRNAs repress target mRNAs
Distinguish miRNA, siRNA and piRNA pathways and RNAi as a research and therapeutic tool
Describe the types and functions of long non-coding RNAs
Explain nonsense-mediated decay as RNA surveillance

keyConcepts.definition: The time for half of a given mRNA population to be degraded; it varies from minutes to many hours between genes.
The major route: poly(A) tail shortening (CCR4-NOT, PAN2-PAN3), then decapping by DCP2 and 5'-3' degradation by XRN1, or 3'-5' decay by the exosome.
An AUUUA-containing sequence in the 3' UTR that binds proteins (such as tristetraprolin) and promotes rapid decay of many cytokine and growth factor mRNAs.
A roughly 22-nucleotide RNA derived from a hairpin precursor that guides an Argonaute-containing RISC to partially complementary sites in mRNAs, mainly in the 3' UTR.
Nucleotides 2-8 of the miRNA, which provide most of the target specificity in animals.
Small interfering RNAs derived from long double-stranded RNA; with perfect complementarity they direct Argonaute-mediated cleavage of the target.
Transcripts longer than about 200 nucleotides with little or no protein-coding capacity; some scaffold chromatin complexes (Xist), others act in the cytoplasm.
A surveillance pathway that degrades mRNAs with premature termination codons, as well as some normal mRNAs.

deeper.beginner: An mRNA is a temporary message, and how long it survives is a key way to control how much protein is made. Some messages are destroyed within minutes, which lets the cell respond quickly, and others last for hours. Tiny RNAs called microRNAs play a part: each one acts like a search term that finds messages with a matching sequence and recruits proteins that block translation or cause the message to be degraded. Scientists have also learned to harness this system, called RNA interference, to silence chosen genes. The 'search term' idea fits well, but a single microRNA can match hundreds of messages, so its effects are broad but usually mild.
deeper.intermediate: In animals, miRNA genes are transcribed by Pol II into primary transcripts that are cleaved by Drosha with DGCR8 to make hairpin pre-miRNAs; Exportin-5 carries them to the cytoplasm, where Dicer cuts them to duplexes. One strand is loaded into Argonaute to form the RISC. Animal miRNAs pair imperfectly through the seed region, and their main effect on targets is to recruit the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex and decapping machinery, with translational repression contributing; plant miRNAs and siRNAs usually pair almost completely and direct cleavage. ARE-binding proteins, other RNA-binding proteins and m6A methylation all tune stability, while NMD removes aberrant transcripts and also adjusts the level of some normal ones. lncRNAs act in many ways, including scaffolds (Xist, HOTAIR), decoys that sponge miRNAs or proteins, and guides; claims of function need experimental support, as many lncRNAs are low abundance and may be transcriptional by-products.
deeper.advanced: Quantitatively, each miRNA typically represses individual targets by less than two-fold, so biological effects arise from sets of targets and from tuning noise, and this fits the observation that many miRNA knockouts show subtle phenotypes. Target prediction by seed matching generates many false positives, and experimental support (CLIP-based mapping, reporter assays with seed mutations) is required. Dicer, Drosha and Argonaute dysfunction in cancers and the use of siRNA drugs (the first approved was patisiran in 2018) show translational importance; delivery and off-target effects remain challenges. The idea that RNAi arose as defence against viruses and transposons, with piRNAs guarding the germline genome, helps connect small RNA pathways to genome integrity. When reading lncRNA papers, ask whether the function was demonstrated by loss-of-function at the DNA level (deletion or CRISPRi) and not only by RNA knockdown, since some effects come from the act of transcription rather than the RNA product.

commonMistakes: Assuming that miRNAs always degrade their targets by cleavage; in animals the dominant effect is deadenylation-linked decay plus translational repression.
Using the terms siRNA and miRNA interchangeably; they differ in origin, precursor structure and usual degree of target complementarity.
Calling any non-coding transcript functional; function has to be demonstrated.
Forgetting that NMD acts on mRNAs that have been translated at least once (the pioneer round).

units.title: Translational control and regulated protein degradation
units.hook: When a cell is starved, infected or overloaded with unfolded protein, it cannot wait for new transcription; it slams the brake on protein synthesis within minutes with a single phosphate group. Then, when a protein is no longer needed, it is tagged with a small molecular label and fed into a shredder.
learningObjectives: Describe the steps of eukaryotic translation initiation and the factors involved
Explain global translational control by eIF2 phosphorylation and by 4E-BPs
Explain selective translational control through uORFs, IRESs and RNA-binding proteins
Contrast bacterial and eukaryotic initiation signals
Describe the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and the principle of regulated degradation
Give examples of proteins whose activity is controlled by degradation

keyConcepts.definition: Eukaryotic initiation in which eIF4E binds the 5' cap, eIF4G bridges to the 43S complex, and the small subunit scans to the first suitable AUG.
eIF2 bound to GTP and initiator Met-tRNA; it delivers the initiator tRNA to the 40S subunit and is recycled by the GEF eIF2B.
Phosphorylation of eIF2 alpha on serine 51 by PERK, GCN2, PKR or HRI, which reduces ternary complex and so lowers global translation while favouring ATF4 translation.
A binding protein that sequesters eIF4E when hypophosphorylated; mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BPs to release eIF4E.
A short open reading frame in the 5' leader that can reduce translation of the main ORF, or under stress allow its increase, as for ATF4 and yeast GCN4.
An RNA structure that recruits ribosomes without a cap, used by some viruses and some cellular mRNAs.
A purine-rich sequence upstream of the start codon in bacterial mRNA that pairs with 16S rRNA to position the ribosome.
Targeted degradation in which E1, E2 and E3 enzymes attach polyubiquitin chains (typically linked through lysine 48) to substrates that are then degraded by the 26S proteasome.
A sequence or modification in a protein that makes it a substrate for a ubiquitin ligase; an example is the N-degron pathway.

deeper.beginner: Making protein is expensive, so the cell regulates it carefully. Most eukaryotic messages begin translation when a protein group grabs the cap at the front of the message and pulls in a ribosome, which then scans along until it finds a start signal. Cells can slow down the whole process by adding a phosphate group to one initiation factor when they are stressed, and can speed it up when nutrients are plentiful. At the other end of a protein's life, a small protein called ubiquitin is attached as a 'send to shredder' tag, and a barrel-shaped machine called the proteasome digests tagged proteins. The shredder picture is good, but the tags are specific: a tiny set of selected proteins is tagged at any one time.
deeper.intermediate: Initiation involves eIF1, eIF1A, eIF3, eIF5 and the ternary complex in a 43S complex that is loaded onto the mRNA by eIF4F (eIF4E, eIF4G, eIF4A); poly(A)-binding protein joins the two ends of the mRNA, helping reinitiation. Scanning continues to an AUG in a good Kozak context, and eIF5B joins the 60S subunit. eIF2 alpha phosphorylation turns eIF2 into a competitive inhibitor of eIF2B, so it takes only a small amount of phosphorylated eIF2 to reduce the active ternary complex; yet some mRNAs, like ATF4, are translated better because of the uORF arrangement. Under growth signalling, mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BPs and increases cap-dependent translation, especially of mRNAs with 5' terminal oligopyrimidine tracts. The ubiquitin cascade uses a single E1, tens of E2s and hundreds of E3s that give substrate specificity; degradation of cyclins and the inhibitor IkB shows how regulated destruction makes irreversible switches.
deeper.advanced: Translational control by eIF2 alpha phosphorylation creates a gene-specific response through leaky scanning and reinitiation: low ternary complex levels allow ribosomes to bypass an inhibitory uORF and reach the ATF4 coding sequence. Ribosome profiling has revealed widespread uORF translation and shown that translation efficiency varies across the transcriptome and differs from mRNA abundance. In bacteria, initiation depends mainly on the Shine-Dalgarno interaction and local mRNA structure, and translational coupling in polycistronic mRNAs and riboswitches provide extra control. For protein degradation, polyubiquitin chain topology encodes different fates (K48 for proteasomal degradation, K63 for signalling), and small molecules called PROTACs exploit E3 ligases to target proteins for degradation, an example of drug design from basic regulation. Interpret half-life data with care: cycloheximide chase assays inhibit translation globally and can alter cell physiology.

commonMistakes: Describing eIF2 alpha phosphorylation as increasing translation; it lowers global translation but increases ATF4.
Mixing up bacterial and eukaryotic initiation: bacteria use Shine-Dalgarno and formyl-methionine, eukaryotes use the cap and scanning with unmodified methionine.
Saying that any ubiquitin tag leads to proteasomal degradation; only specific chain types do.
Assuming that mRNA with an IRES is always translated more; efficiency is context-dependent.

units.title: From signal to gene: hormones, development and disease
units.hook: A steroid hormone slips through the cell membrane, finds its receptor and, within minutes, rewrites which genes are on. The same principle, scaled up across a growing embryo, draws the body plan, and when it fails it can create a tumour.
learningObjectives: Describe how nuclear receptors act as ligand-regulated transcription factors
Explain how signalling pathways converge on transcription factors (CREB, NF-kB, STATs, SMADs)
Explain how morphogen gradients and combinatorial enhancers pattern the Drosophila embryo
Describe the role of Hox genes in body plan
Give examples of gene regulation defects in cancer and how regulation is targeted therapeutically

keyConcepts.definition: A ligand-activated transcription factor with a zinc-finger DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain; examples include glucocorticoid, oestrogen, thyroid hormone and retinoic acid receptors.
A short DNA sequence recognised by a nuclear receptor, often as a palindromic or direct repeat half-site pair.
Unliganded receptors such as thyroid hormone receptor can bind corepressors with HDAC activity; ligand binding changes receptor conformation so coactivators with HAT activity replace them.
A factor whose activity is controlled by phosphorylation, proteolysis or nuclear translocation in response to a signal, such as CREB, NF-kB, STAT and SMAD.
A concentration gradient of a signalling or regulatory molecule (for example Bicoid in Drosophila) that gives different gene responses at different positions.
A family of homeodomain transcription factors arranged in clusters whose order on the chromosome mirrors their expression along the head-to-tail axis (colinearity).
A transcription factor that drives cancer when overexpressed, mutated or fused, for example MYC amplification or PML-RARA in acute promyelocytic leukaemia.
A drug targeting chromatin regulators, such as HDAC inhibitors or DNA methyltransferase inhibitors used in some haematological cancers.

deeper.beginner: Cells constantly receive messages from their surroundings, and many of these messages end by switching particular genes on or off. Some hormones like cortisol are fat-soluble and pass directly into the cell, where they bind a receptor that acts as a transcription factor. Others bind receptors at the cell surface and set off a relay that finally activates a transcription factor in the nucleus. In an embryo, gradients of such regulators tell cells where they are along the body, so that the head, thorax and abdomen develop in the right places. The idea that the cell simply 'receives instructions' is incomplete: cells also interpret the same signal differently depending on which factors they already carry.
deeper.intermediate: Steroid receptors such as the glucocorticoid receptor are held in the cytoplasm by heat shock proteins; hormone binding releases them, they dimerise, enter the nucleus and bind response elements, where they recruit coactivators and chromatin remodellers. Thyroid hormone and retinoid receptors are generally already on DNA (as heterodimers with RXR) and repress transcription until ligand arrives. Other pathways converge on factors by different mechanisms: PKA phosphorylates CREB, which recruits CBP; inflammatory signals trigger degradation of IkB so that NF-kB enters the nucleus; cytokine receptors activate JAK kinases that phosphorylate STATs; TGF-beta receptors phosphorylate SMADs. In Drosophila, maternal Bicoid forms an anterior-to-posterior gradient and activates gap genes at different thresholds; gap proteins and pair-rule enhancers (as in the even-skipped stripe 2 enhancer) integrate positive and negative inputs to make sharp stripes. Hox genes then specify segment identity, and mutations can transform one body part into another.
deeper.advanced: Enhancers are modular, so a single gene can be controlled by multiple enhancers each driving a part of its pattern, and this modularity is thought to be central to the evolution of morphology because it allows changes in one tissue without affecting others. Transcription factor concentration thresholds, cooperativity and repression by short-range repressors such as Kruppel and Giant convert smooth gradients into discrete domains. In disease, non-coding variation in enhancers is a major component of GWAS signals, and tumours often show 'enhancer hijacking' by chromosomal rearrangements or super-enhancers driving oncogenes like MYC. Therapeutically, all-trans retinoic acid and arsenic trioxide target PML-RARA in APL and are among the most successful examples of treating a transcription factor defect, while BET bromodomain inhibitors and HDAC inhibitors target the chromatin reading and writing machinery; resistance and toxicity illustrate that regulators with broad roles are difficult targets.

commonMistakes: Assuming all nuclear receptors start in the cytoplasm; thyroid and retinoid receptors are typically nuclear and DNA-bound without ligand.
Treating signalling pathways as linear lines; extensive crosstalk and feedback shape the final output.
Calling Hox genes 'master switches' of organs; they specify positional identity and act with other factors.
Concluding from correlation that an enhancer variant causes disease without testing the regulatory effect.
